transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

Hi. Thank you so much for seeing me. Um, well, I suppose occupational health actually sent me here. I really hope I'm not taking up a spot from someone who needs it more, but... they were a bit concerned because I've gotten into this sort of pattern lately. 

With my work, I just tend to push breakfast and lunch aside during long lab runs or exhibition work. You just get so focused on the research, you know? And then, by the time I finally do eat, I just keep it to something very small and... well, controlled. It’s just easier to manage my day that way, I guess. I hope that makes sense?
Do you feel distressed or find that your eating habits are affecting other areas of your life, like your work or relationships?

Oh, um, distressed? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, work is going fine. I'm still meeting all my main deadlines, which is the most important thing, right? I always make sure the work gets done. 

But... well, I suppose I have sort of stopped going to the lab lunches lately. And those informal gallery planning meals we sometimes have. It’s just... it’s easier to stay at my desk and keep working rather than trying to navigate the food there, you know? I guess it does mean I’m a bit more isolated from my colleagues than I used to be... but it’s really not a huge problem, I promise. I'm still doing my job well. Does that... does that answer your question okay?
Do you find that your weight or the way you look affects how you feel about yourself overall?

Oh, um... I guess it does, a little bit? I mean, I know I shouldn't let it bother me, especially at my age, and I really try not to be vain about these things. But... well, when I'm getting ready for the lab in the morning and I look in the mirror, I just... I don't see someone who looks thin or put-together. 

I mostly just end up focusing on, um, my stomach or my hips. And it just makes me feel like I look... I don't know, careless? Or like I'm not a serious professional. In my field, you want to look sharp and disciplined, and I just feel like those areas make me look the opposite. I know it sounds silly to worry about that when I should just be thinking about my research. I'm sorry, I hope that doesn't sound too superficial?
Do you ever do anything to try to compensate for the food you eat, like making yourself sick, using laxatives, or exercising a lot more than you should?

Oh, no, no, I don't do anything like that. I would never... making myself sick or taking things like laxatives, that's just... no, I definitely don't do that. I know that can be really dangerous, and I try to be very responsible about my health, I really do. 

And as for exercise, I mean, I just do normal things. I walk to the lab, and sometimes I'll go for a walk in the evening if I need to clear my head after staring at data all day. But it's nothing extreme, I promise. Just... just regular activity to stay a bit healthy. Is that... is that the sort of thing you were asking about? I hope I'm giving you the right information.

Do you ever find yourself eating a very large amount of food in a short period, more than you would normally eat under similar circumstances, and feel like you can't stop or control how much you're eating?

Oh, um... no. No, I definitely don't do that. I'm actually very careful about what I eat, so the idea of just... losing control like that and eating huge amounts... that doesn't really happen to me. 

I try to be very disciplined, you know? Especially with my work, I have to be so precise, and I think that just carries over into how I manage my meals. I prefer to keep things very structured and planned out. I would feel awful if I just let myself go like that. I hope that makes sense? I'm trying to be as helpful as I can with your questions.

How much does your eating behavior relate to concerns about your body shape or weight? For example, is avoiding eating certain foods or controlling your portions mainly about managing your weight or changing your body shape?

Oh, um... well, I suppose it is related, yes. I mean, I wouldn't say it's an obsession or anything like that, but... I do like to keep a close eye on things. 

It's just that, um... well, if I step on the scale and it goes up, even just a tiny fraction of a pound, I... I get this sudden, sharp panic. It just makes me feel like I'm completely losing my grip on the discipline I've worked so incredibly hard to maintain. And I know that probably sounds a bit silly, worrying over a fraction of a number, but it really does frighten me to think I might be slipping up. 

So, yes, I suppose controlling my portions is a way to make sure that doesn't happen. I just want to make sure I'm staying on track and not letting things get out of hand. Is that... is that a normal way to feel? I hope I'm explaining it alright.
Have you lost a significant amount of weight recently, or do you currently weigh much less than you used to, even if it wasn’t intentional?

Oh, um... well, I suppose I have lost a little bit of weight, yes. I wouldn't say it's anything alarming, though, I promise. I don't want you to think I'm doing anything drastic. It's just... well, I have noticed that my clothes are quite a bit looser lately. And, yes, the numbers on the scale have kept drifting down over the last few months. 

But, to be completely honest with you—and I hope this doesn't sound bad—part of me actually sees that as a sign that I'm staying really focused. Things at the lab have been incredibly chaotic recently, and seeing those numbers go down just... it makes me feel like I'm not letting all that stress and chaos spill over into my body. It shows I still have discipline, you know? 

Is that... does that make sense to you? I really just want to make sure I'm managing everything properly, and I hope it's alright that I look at it that way.
When you look in the mirror, do you see yourself as larger or heavier than you actually are, even when others might not notice any significant difference?

Oh, um... well, I wouldn't say I see myself as... as huge or anything like that. I really don't want to sound like I'm completely out of touch with reality. But, um... it's just that when I'm getting ready in the morning, before I head to the lab, and I look in the mirror... I definitely don't see someone who is, you know, thin. 

My eyes just sort of... they immediately go to my stomach or my hips. And to me, they just look... well, they make me feel like I look careless, or like I'm not taking myself seriously enough. In my field, you have to present yourself so professionally, and I just worry that if I look a certain way, it might reflect poorly on my work ethic. 

I know other people might not see it that way, and I really hope I don't sound vain or obsessed with my appearance. It's more about just wanting to look put-together and disciplined. Do you think that's a fair way to look at it? I hope I'm answering your question properly.
Can you tell me approximately how much you currently weigh, and how tall you are?

Oh, um... well, I suppose I can tell you that. I just... I don't want you to be concerned, because I really do feel fine. I'm about five foot six, and... well, the last time I checked, I think I was around... maybe 105 pounds? 

I know that might sound a little bit on the lower side, but I promise I'm eating, and I have plenty of energy for my work at the lab. It's just a number, really. I hope that's... I hope that's an okay weight for someone my height? I just want to make sure I'm doing everything I'm supposed to be doing.
Was losing weight a goal for you, or has the weight loss happened without you specifically trying to lose weight?

Oh, um... well, it wasn't exactly a... a strict goal at first, I suppose. I didn't set out with a specific number in mind, I promise. It started more as just trying to eat cleaner and be more mindful, you know, to handle the stress at the lab better. 

But... well, I guess as time went on, it did become something I actively tried to maintain. And now... to be perfectly honest, and I hope this doesn't sound too strange... the thought of gaining it back is actually quite terrifying. If the scale goes up even a tiny fraction of a pound, I feel this... this really sharp panic. It just feels like I'm losing all the discipline I've worked so incredibly hard to build. 

I just want to stay in control of things, you know? Does that make sense? I hope it doesn't make me sound unreasonable... I just want to make sure I'm doing the right thing.
Have you ever intentionally kept your weight below what you know is a healthy range for your height, even if it meant restricting food significantly or feeling hungry most of the time?

Oh, goodness, no. Um... I really wouldn't want to do anything that I know is medically unhealthy. I mean, especially with my background in biology, I... I understand how the body works, and I definitely wouldn't intentionally do something to damage it. 

And I don't really feel hungry most of the time, either. I think my body has just sort of... adapted to the portions I eat now. I make sure I have enough to get through my day at the lab without losing focus or feeling faint. If I really need something, I'll have a sensible snack. I would never want to just starve myself... that sounds so irresponsible, doesn't it? 

I really am trying to take good care of myself and be sensible about it, I promise. I hope you don't think I'm doing something dangerous?
Would you say that your eating habits are mainly influenced by a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, even if you don’t necessarily see yourself as larger than you are?

Oh, um... well, I suppose it's a bit like what I mentioned a few minutes ago... about how if the scale goes up even a tiny fraction, I get that really sharp panic. But I wouldn't necessarily call it a fear of becoming fat. That just sounds so... well, so superficial, and I really hope you don't think I'm a vain person. 

It's more just that... I'm terrified of losing the discipline I've worked so very hard to maintain. So I guess that panic does guide my eating habits, yes, because I just want to keep everything perfectly in balance and not lose my grip on things. I really hope that doesn't make me sound obsessive or anything... I just value being disciplined and taking my health seriously, you know? Is that... is it okay that I look at it that way?
Would you say that your efforts to control your eating are mainly driven by a desire to become thinner or to prevent yourself from gaining any weight, even if it's just a small amount?

Um... yes, I suppose it is mostly about preventing the weight gain. Like I was trying to explain a moment ago, I really don't want you to think I'm just trying to be as thin as possible for... well, for vanity's sake. It's not about that at all, I promise. 

It's just... as I mentioned before, if I see the number on the scale creep up even the tiniest fraction, that's when that awful panic sets in. It just feels like a failure, like all that careful discipline I've built up is just slipping away from me. I'm not trying to disappear or anything like that, I just want to keep everything steady and perfectly controlled so I don't lose my progress. 

That makes sense, right? It's a perfectly normal thing to want to maintain the hard work you've put into yourself, isn't it?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If the scale goes up even a fraction, I feel this sharp panic that I’m losing the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the eating habits are mainly influenced by a fear of gaining weight or becoming fat, which directly corresponds to the Fear_of_Weight_Gain symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Oh, um... well, I suppose it's a bit like what I mentioned a few minutes ago... about how if the scale goes up even a tiny fraction, I get that really sharp panic. But I wouldn't necessarily call it a fear of becoming fat. That just sounds so... well, so superficial, and I really hope you don't think I'm a vain person. 

It's more just that... I'm terrified of losing the discipline I've worked so very hard to maintain. So I guess that panic does guide my eating habits, yes, because I just want to keep everything perfectly in balance and not lose my grip on things. I really hope that doesn't make me sound obsessive or anything... I just value being disciplined and taking my health seriously, you know? Is that... is it okay that I look at it that way?

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's weight loss and eating habits are driven by a fear of gaining weight or a desire to be thin, which would help differentiate between Anorexia Nervosa (F50.00) and Other Specified Feeding or Eating Disorder (F51.80).
doctor.question: Would you say that your efforts to control your eating are mainly driven by a desire to become thinner or to prevent yourself from gaining any weight, even if it's just a small amount?

target_item.name: Fear_of_Weight_Gain
target_item.manifestation: If the scale goes up even a fraction, I feel this sharp panic that I’m losing the discipline I’ve worked so hard to maintain.
target_item.reason: The doctor is again asking about the motivation behind controlling eating, specifically whether it is driven by a desire to become thinner or prevent weight gain (even a small amount). This directly maps to the intense fear of gaining weight.

patient.answer:
Um... yes, I suppose it is mostly about preventing the weight gain. Like I was trying to explain a moment ago, I really don't want you to think I'm just trying to be as thin as possible for... well, for vanity's sake. It's not about that at all, I promise. 

It's just... as I mentioned before, if I see the number on the scale creep up even the tiniest fraction, that's when that awful panic sets in. It just feels like a failure, like all that careful discipline I've built up is just slipping away from me. I'm not trying to disappear or anything like that, I just want to keep everything steady and perfectly controlled so I don't lose my progress. 

That makes sense, right? It's a perfectly normal thing to want to maintain the hard work you've put into yourself, isn't it?

inference.note: The patient's responses indicate a preoccupation with weight gain, significant weight loss, and restrictive eating behaviors driven by a fear of gaining weight and a desire to maintain control, despite not explicitly endorsing body image distortion. These features are most consistent with anorexia nervosa (F50.00). Other candidates such as F51.80 (nonorganic insomnia) are no longer supported given the depth of information about eating behaviors, weight concerns, and psychopathology.

opening_question.intent: Identify the patient's chief complaint or reason for seeking help
opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. Can you tell me what brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient meets diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa, restricting type, based on persistent restriction of food intake, intense fear of gaining weight, disturbance in self-perceived weight or shape, and significantly low body weight for height. Other differential diagnoses including atypical anorexia and obsessive-compulsive disorder were considered but ruled out based on the full clinical picture.
